design_detail: One-year (calendar 2010) population cohort of all North Carolina residents (9,560,234), built from linked administrative records: the state Controlled Substances Reporting System (prescription monitoring; 54,825,930 dispensing records for 2009-2011, 7,393,375 opioid analgesic records after cleaning) and death certificates with Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) records, linked by name and date of birth. The authors call it a prospective cohort; the records were assembled and analysed afterwards, and for people who died, exposure time was counted back from death (first prescription in the 365 days before death). Exposure: average daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) from dispensed prescriptions (intent-to-treat); outcome: unintentional or undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths in which a medical examiner judged an opioid analgesic to have a primary or additive role (629 deaths); crude rates by MME stratum from Poisson models (generalized estimating equations); benzodiazepine exposure: any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study. Read in full from the PDF (Pain Med 2016;17:85-98); Table 1 and Figure 5 caption checked on rendered pages 90 and 93; Figures 2 to 4 are images and their values were not read.
can_establish: How overdose death rates involving opioid analgesics in North Carolina in 2010 varied by average prescribed daily dose (crude rates and rate ratios against the lowest-dose group); how many such deaths had a benzodiazepine, alcohol, cocaine or heroin judged involved by the medical examiner; and how many of the people who died had been dispensed an opioid painkiller in the previous year.
cannot_establish: Whether higher doses or co-dispensed benzodiazepines caused the deaths (nothing is adjusted: not age, sex, reason for prescribing, other illness or other drugs, and higher doses go to sicker patients); how much risk a benzodiazepine adds for a person taking both (the rate ratio of about 10 is crude and cannot be reproduced from the numbers printed); when in the year risk falls (assumed constant); deaths involving opioids obtained outside the monitoring programme; anything about illicit opioids.

sample.recruitment: Records: all residents alive in 2010, from the state's mid-year population estimate; prescriptions from the Controlled Substances Reporting System; deaths from the State Center for Health Statistics and the OCME (Methods > Study Design; Data Sources; Statistical Analysis).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Residents who died in 2010 with an underlying cause of unintentional or undetermined drug overdose (ICD-10 X40-X44, Y10-Y14) and an opioid analgesic judged involved in a primary or additive role; deaths with opioids present but judged circumstantial were excluded; suicides excluded. Toxicology records were available for 824 (92%) of the overdose deaths identified from vital statistics. The monitoring programme omits Veterans Administration and Department of Defense pharmacies, Indian Health Service clinics, in-clinic dispensing by physicians and outpatient opioid dependence treatment programmes (Methods > Data Sources, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records-based). About 8% of identified overdose deaths lacked toxicology records and could not be classified (editors' reading of 824 (92%)).
sample.demographics: Decedents: 37.2% female (234), median age 43 years (interquartile range 32-51). Patients: 22.8% of residents were dispensed an opioid analgesic; 2.8% of those patients (61,879) averaged more than 150 mg/day MME; 89.6% of licensed clinicians prescribed an opioid analgesic and 40.0% an extended-release one. No characteristics of patients other than prescribing patterns are given (Results, pp. 89-90).
sample.selection_effects: A whole-state population, so selection is mainly by what the monitoring programme records: opioids from other states or non-medical sources are not seen (p. 94). The 151 deaths (24.0%) with no opioid analgesic dispensed in the previous year are counted in the numerator but cannot belong to any dose group, and unexposed person-years (3,554,850) are under half the unexposed people (7,377,860), unexplained (reporting issue 6).

exposure.measurement: Dispensed prescriptions (strength, quantity, days' supply, formulation) converted to MME with CDC factors (codeine 0.15, fentanyl 25.0, hydrocodone 1.0, hydromorphone 4.0, methadone 3.0, morphine 1.0, oxycodone 1.5, oxymorphone 3.0); average daily MME = total MME divided by days' supply, with overlapping prescriptions taken into account; days' supply was missing or zero for 10% of records and imputed by median for the same quantity and product (Methods > Exposure Definition, pp. 87-88).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: prescribed average daily dose in 16 strata, from more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day MME (reference) up to 500 to 5,000 mg/day; dispensed, not taken: the authors assume each prescription was taken as directed (Limitations, p. 94).
exposure.polysubstance: Benzodiazepine dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study (any, yes or no) was examined as a modifier; medical examiners judged benzodiazepines involved in 61.4% (386) of the 629 deaths, ethanol in 12.2% (77), cocaine in 8.4% (53) and heroin in 1.3% (8). Nothing is adjusted for other drugs (Results, p. 89; Methods, p. 88).

comparison.controls: Unexposed residents (no opioid analgesic dispensed in 2010): 151 deaths and 3,554,850 person-years in Table 1. Rate ratios use the lowest exposed stratum (more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day; 98 deaths, 1,305,835 person-years) as the reference.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The reasons opioids and benzodiazepines were prescribed (pain, injury, psychiatric disorder, substance use disorder), illness severity, age, sex, prior overdose, duration of therapy and other drugs: the authors say none was controlled for, that patients at higher doses are more likely to have more serious illness, and name exchangeability across doses as the greatest limitation (p. 94).

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates (underlying cause X40-X44, Y10-Y14) with OCME toxicology and investigation records; each drug's role in the death classified by OCME toxicologists as primary (concentration enough to have caused the death alone) or additive (not enough alone but acting with other drugs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The role of each drug is the examiners' judgment, which the authors say 'inherently contains an element of subjective clinical judgment' (p. 94); whether examiners knew the person's prescriptions is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Any overdose death in which at least one of eight named opioid analgesics was judged involved in a primary or additive role; benzodiazepine and ethanol involvement by the same examiners' judgment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; descriptive rates and rate ratios with 95% intervals in 16 dose strata and two benzodiazepine groups.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; examiners classified deaths independently of this study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Crude rates from deaths and person-years: 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022%). Printed rate ratios against more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day: 2.6 (95% CI 2.0-3.5) at 40-59.9; 6.2 (4.2-9.2) at 80-99.9; 6.7 (4.3-10.6) at 100-119.9; 14.1 (8.9-22.5) at 120-139.9; 29.5 (17.1-50.7) at 160-179.9; 27.4 (17.5-42.8) at 200-249.9; 90.4 (60.7-134.6) at 500-5,000 mg/day; unexposed 0.57 (0.44-0.73); no distinct threshold at 100 or 120 mg/day. Benzodiazepines: crude rate 7.0 (6.3-7.8) per 10,000 person-years among patients co-dispensed benzodiazepines against 0.7 (0.6-0.9) with opioid analgesics alone, about ten times higher; the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years at more than 0 to 74.9 mg/day, rising to 45.8 at 300 to 5,000 mg/day (Figure 5, image). Editors' checks: the printed rates in Table 1 exceed deaths divided by person-years in every exposed stratum (reference stratum 1.3 printed against 0.75 calculated from 98 deaths and 1,305,835 person-years; highest stratum 80.0 against 68.3) while the printed rate ratios match ratios of the calculated rates (500-5,000 mg/day: 91.0 calculated against 90.4 printed); the unexposed rate prints as 0.34 against 0.42 calculated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration; the hypothesis that part of the dose-dependent risk comes from co-prescribed benzodiazepines is stated at the end of the Introduction (p. 86).
analysis.selective_reporting: The benzodiazepine rates are in the text and Figure 5 only; no table gives deaths, person-years or rates by dose and benzodiazepine status, and the 7.0 and 0.7 rates have no counts printed.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the five highest dose strata have 14 to 32 deaths each, and the intervals are wide.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In North Carolina in 2010, 629 overdose deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role according to medical examiners: 478 in people dispensed an opioid analgesic in the year (about 2.2 per 10,000 person-years, editors' calculation) and 151 in people with none. Crude death rates rose steadily with average daily dose, without a visible jump at 100 or 120 mg/day, to a rate ratio near 90 at 500 mg/day or more, against the lowest dose group. Medical examiners judged benzodiazepines involved in 61.4% of the 629 deaths and ethanol in 12.2%; 80% of patients had been dispensed a benzodiazepine in the previous year; crude death rates were about ten times higher among patients dispensed both than with opioids alone, with a gap that widened at higher doses.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says half of the 629 deaths had an opioid analgesic prescription active on the day of death; that risk 'increased gradually and did not show evidence of a distinct risk threshold'; and calls for guidance on combined classes of medicines. The discussion says the dose-dependent relationship 'is strongly influenced by' concurrent benzodiazepine exposure; the conclusion says much of the risk at higher doses appears to be associated with co-prescribed benzodiazepines and speaks of dangerous situations created by 'ignoring known drug interactions' at the point of care. Gaps: (1) nothing is adjusted, so 'strongly influenced' and 'much of the risk' rest on crude rate differences that sicker patients taking both drugs would also show; (2) the half is 244 of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid (51%), or 39% of all 629; (3) 'ignoring known drug interactions' treats co-prescribing as the cause; (4) the benzodiazepine rates cannot be reproduced from the numbers given (reporting issue 2).

timeline.event: Paulozzi and colleagues (Pain Med), as quoted by this paper (not read): odds ratios of 12.2 for 40 to 120 mg/day and 11.3 for the highest categories, against a combined unexposed and low-dose group, with a similar curve shape

Fulton-Kehoe and colleagues (Med Care), Washington State Medicaid, as quoted by this paper (not read): 44.5% of methadone poisoning decedents and 48% of other opioid decedents had a sedative prescription in the month before death; 26% and 16% had no opioid prescription

Park and colleagues (BMJ), case-cohort of US veterans receiving opioid analgesics: this paper quotes 27% of patients also receiving benzodiazepines and 49% of decedents with both prescriptions; the full paper, read separately in this library, reports an adjusted hazard ratio for overdose death of 3.86 (95% CI 3.49-4.26) during benzodiazepine prescription against none

Sun and colleagues, privately insured adults aged 18 to 64 (read separately in this library): adjusted odds ratio 2.14 (95% CI 2.05-2.24) for a hospital-treated opioid overdose in years with at least one day of overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions, against years without

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the finding (more overdose deaths where benzodiazepines are also prescribed, higher with higher opioid doses) agrees with the adjusted cohorts read for this library (Park and colleagues; Sun and colleagues); the size reported here (about tenfold) is crude and cannot be used. The finding that no clear risk threshold appears at 100 or 120 mg/day is from this single analysis, with unadjusted rates.

funding.funder: Dasgupta's time was partly funded by grants from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Public Health Law Research programme (for analysis) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U01CE002162, for publication support); the funding organizations had no direct role in the study. The work was done as part of a doctoral dissertation (p. 85; Acknowledgments, p. 95).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dasgupta is employed by Epidemico, Inc., a public health software company with no direct contracts with opioid manufacturers (as of 1 May 2015), and served on a Risk Safety Advisory Board for Covidien, dissolved in August 2012; no other author has disclosures (p. 85).
funding.affiliations_note: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (Epidemiology; Injury Prevention Research Center; Health Behavior); North Carolina Division of Public Health (Injury and Violence Prevention Branch), which also supplied the death data; CDC/CSTE Applied Epidemiology Fellowship.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort with individual-level covariates (age, sex, diagnoses, prior psychiatric and substance use treatment, other medicines) and time-varying exposure to opioid dose and to concurrent benzodiazepine days' supply, a design that starts follow-up when people first begin a medicine, or compares two active treatments, and a self-controlled analysis comparing each person's periods with and without benzodiazepines; with death classification by examiners blind to prescriptions, and counts printed for every rate.

domains.note: No covariate is used. For the benzodiazepine contrast (about ten times higher crude rate; 80% of patients exposed) the exposed and comparison groups differ in reasons for prescribing, illness and substance use; for the dose contrast alone this would be high, since higher doses go to sicker patients (the authors' greatest limitation, p. 94).

Dispensed, not taken; 10% of days' supply imputed; the monitoring programme omits several sources; the Methods define benzodiazepine exposure by person (any dispensing in 365 days) but the printed rates imply a much smaller exposed person-time (reporting issue 2).

Whole-state population, a strength; person-time for decedents starts at the first prescription in the 365 days before death while for survivors it starts at the first prescription in 2010; unexposed and total person-years are unexplained (reporting issue 6).
Intent-to-treat classification and an assumption of constant risk across the year, which the authors say is unlikely to hold at higher doses (risk may be highest shortly after starting).
About 8% of identified overdose deaths lacked toxicology records; 10% of days' supply imputed; no covariate data to be missing.

Medical examiners' judgment of a primary or additive role, with whether they knew the prescriptions unstated; an examiner's finding of benzodiazepine involvement may be likelier when a benzodiazepine prescription is known.
No registration; Table 1 rates do not match its own deaths and person-years; benzodiazepine rates shown without counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The descriptive findings (how many deaths, the share with a benzodiazepine or alcohol judged involved, the share of decedents with an opioid prescription) are not affected by confounding and may be cited as what these medical examiners judged in North Carolina in 2010, with the counts' limits stated. The comparative findings are unadjusted: the dose-specific rate ratios and especially the ten-fold benzodiazepine rate ratio are too confounded to estimate any effect, and the benzodiazepine rates cannot be reproduced from the paper's own numbers. The study may not be cited for how much a benzodiazepine or a higher dose adds to risk, or for the absence of a threshold at 100 mg/day.

key_findings.finding: Design and results in the abstract: a prospective observational cohort with one year of follow-up of the North Carolina residential population (9,560,234; 2,182,374 opioid analgesic patients); 629 overdose deaths, half with an active opioid analgesic prescription on the day of death; 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022% per year); rates rose gradually across daily MME; 80.0% of patients also received benzodiazepines; death rates among those co-dispensed benzodiazepines and opioids were ten times higher (7.0 per 10,000 person-years, CI 6.3 to 7.8) than with opioids alone (0.7, CI 0.6 to 0.9).
key_findings.note: 'Half' is 244 of 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid, not of 629.

key_findings.finding: Data: the prescription monitoring programme (since 2007) captures pharmacy dispensing in the state but omits Veterans Administration and Department of Defense pharmacies, Indian Health Service clinics, in-clinic dispensing by physicians, veterinary clinics and outpatient opioid dependence treatment programmes. Deaths come from death certificates supplemented by OCME records; post-mortem toxicology is done as part of autopsy.

For each overdose decedent, prescriptions dispensed in the 365 days before death were identified by linking the first five letters of the last name and date of birth, then confirmed with first name, full last name and date of birth.

Exposure: dispensed solid oral or transdermal opioid analgesics (codeine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl, methadone, morphine, oxycodone, oxymorphone), converted to MME with CDC factors; days' supply imputed for 10% of records; average daily MME from total MME over days' supply with overlaps; benzodiazepine exposure dichotomised as any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study.

Outcome: underlying cause of unintentional or undetermined drug overdose (X40-X44, Y10-Y14); OCME toxicologists classified each drug as having a primary or additive role from scene investigation, toxicology, records and interviews; deaths with opioids merely present were excluded; records were abstracted for decedents with toxicology available, 824 (92%) of the deaths identified.

Analysis: person-time accrued in 2010 or in the 365 days before death; intent-to-treat exposure from the first opioid prescription; incidence rates and rate ratios from Poisson regression with person-days as offset, generalized estimating equations; no covariates.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 89); no covariates: Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 94)

key_findings.finding: 2,182,374 residents (22.8%) were dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010; hydrocodone to 70% of patients and oxycodone to 39%; 89.6% of licensed clinicians prescribed opioid analgesics and 40.0% an extended-release formulation; 61,879 patients (2.8%) averaged more than 150 mg/day MME.

629 deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role; 37.2% were female and median age was 43; ethanol was judged involved in 12.2% (77), cocaine in 8.4% (53) and heroin in 1.3% (8); 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022%).

Half of decedents (51%, 244) had a current opioid analgesic prescription on the day of death; among the 629 deaths, 24.0% (151) had no opioid analgesic dispensed in the previous 365 days; of the 478 with an opioid, 43.1% had received at least one extended-release formulation.
key_findings.note: The percentage of 51 is of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid; of all 629 it is 38.8% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Dose-dependent risk: incidence rates rose gradually and stayed elevated beyond 200 mg/day MME; no distinct threshold at 100 or 120 mg/day. Table 1 gives, against more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day, rate ratios of 6.7 (4.3-10.6) at 100-119.9, 27.4 (17.5-42.8) at 200-249.9 and 90.4 (60.7-134.6) at 500-5,000 mg/day, based on 23, 24 and 32 deaths in those strata and 98 in the reference stratum.
key_findings.locator: Results > Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 1st paragraph (p. 90); Table 1 (p. 93)
key_findings.note: Table 1 values checked on a rendered page; the printed rates do not match deaths divided by person-years (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines were dispensed in the past year to 80.0% (1,747,166) of opioid analgesic patients and judged involved by medical examiners in 61.4% (386) of the 629 deaths; crude death rates were about ten times higher with both (7.0 per 10,000 person-years) than with opioid analgesics alone (0.7); compared with patients at the same MME, the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years at more than 0 to 74.9 mg/day, rising to 45.8 at 300 to 5,000 mg/day.
key_findings.locator: Results > Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 2nd paragraph; Figure 5 (p. 93, image)

key_findings.finding: The authors call the 80% a surprise, compared with 5% of the US adult population receiving benzodiazepines; they quote Washington State Medicaid (44.5% of methadone poisoning decedents and 48% of other opioid decedents with a sedative prescription in the month before death) and US veterans (27% of patients also received benzodiazepines; 49% of decedents had both prescriptions), and say differences between studies are probably due to the time definitions used.

Limitations named: the model assumes continuous risk during exposed and unexposed time, unlikely at higher doses (risk may be highest soon after starting; duration of therapy not considered); medical examiner determination 'inherently contains an element of subjective clinical judgment'; opioids from other states or non-medical sources are unseen; dispensed doses assumed taken as directed; many high-dose immediate-release opioids contain acetaminophen; the greatest limitation is exchangeability, since patients at higher doses are likely to have more serious illness, with no covariates available to adjust for it.

Conclusion: higher doses were associated with increased overdose risk with smaller incremental increases above 200 mg/day MME; much of the risk at higher doses 'appears to be associated with' co-prescribed benzodiazepines; the authors call for understanding what level of extended-release prescribing balances access and overdose risk and say dangerous situations arise 'by ignoring known drug interactions at the point of care'.

reporting_issues.issue: The rates per 10,000 person-years printed in Table 1 are higher than deaths divided by person-years in every exposed stratum (reference stratum: 1.3 printed against 0.75 from 98 deaths and 1,305,835 person-years; 100-119.9: 8.3 against 5.05; 500-5,000: 80.0 against 68.3), and the unexposed rate is lower (0.34 printed, 0.42 calculated), while the printed rate ratios match the ratio of the calculated rates (for example 90.4 printed against 91.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: The rates and rate ratios in the same table cannot both be right as printed; use counts and person-years, not the rate column.

reporting_issues.issue: The benzodiazepine-stratified rates cannot be reproduced. The Methods classify benzodiazepine exposure by person (any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study) and 80% of patients (1,747,166) were exposed; at 7.0 per 10,000 person-years that implies more than 1,200 deaths (0.8 x 2,181,847 person-years x 7.0 per 10,000, editors' calculation), more than the 478 deaths among patients and the 629 in all. The printed intervals imply a few hundred deaths and a much smaller exposed person-time.
reporting_issues.consequence: How benzodiazepine exposure was timed in the rate calculation is not stated; the ten-fold contrast should not be quoted as a rate ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says there were 629 deaths, half of which had an opioid analgesic prescription active on the day of death, and the text says half of all decedents; the 51% is 244 of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid, and 244 of 629 is 38.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote the proportion with its denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The 80.0% of patients dispensed a benzodiazepine in a year is about three times the 27% the paper quotes for US veterans, and implies that 18% of all North Carolina residents (0.228 x 0.80) were dispensed one, against the 5% of US adults the paper quotes; the paper calls the 80% 'surprising', puts differences between studies down to time definitions, and does not list which drugs counted as benzodiazepines.
reporting_issues.consequence: The benzodiazepine classification may be wider than expected; treat the 80% and the ten-fold contrast with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion and conclusion say the dose-dependent relationship is 'strongly influenced' by benzodiazepines and that much of the risk at higher doses appears associated with them; no model includes benzodiazepines or tests an interaction, and nothing is adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are interpretation of crude rate differences, not results.

reporting_issues.issue: Person-years do not match the population: the total of 5,736,696 is 60% of the 9,560,234 residents followed for a year, the 3,554,850 unexposed person-years are under half of the 7,377,860 unexposed residents who the Methods say contributed person-days for all of 2010, and the exposed person-years (2,181,847) almost equal the number of patients (2,182,374), although the Methods count exposure from each patient's first prescription in 2010, which would give most patients less than a full year.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators, and so every rate, cannot be reconstructed from the Methods.

reporting_issues.issue: The captions of Figures 4 and 5 give the reference group as more than 0 to 19.9 mg/day, whereas Table 1 and the text use more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day; the Discussion gives rate ratios of 'IRR ranging from 16.6 through 90.4' for the highest categories, and 16.6 does not appear in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference group for the figures is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is labelled prospective but the records were assembled and analysed after the deaths, and for decedents exposure time was counted back from death while for survivors it was counted forward from the first prescription in 2010.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treated here as a retrospective cohort; the different time starts for decedents and survivors could bias rates.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 85-98 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Dasgupta_2016_HighDoseOpioidOverdoseMortalityCohort.pdf), full text including abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, Table 1, figure legends, disclosures, acknowledgments and reference list; Table 1 and the Figure 5 caption checked on rendered pages 90 and 93; Figures 2 to 5 are images and no values were read from them. Rates and ratios were recalculated from the printed counts and person-years.
